claim: DNA replication fork stalling is a major cause of genomic instability that underlies many human genetic diseases, from cancer to antibiotic resistance.
source: DNA replication fork stalling is now recognized as a major cause of the genomic instability that underlies many human genetic diseases, from cancer to antibiotic resistance (Tubbs and Nussenzweig, 2017; Zeman and Cimprich, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Tubbs and Nussenzweig, 2017; Zeman and Cimprich, 2014).

claim: Replication factories have been observed in all three domains of life.
source: Remarkably, replication factories have been observed in all three domains of life (Li et al., 2020), yet the functional advantage(s) of this relationship are unknown.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2020.

claim: The functional advantage(s) of replication factories are unknown.
source: Remarkably, replication factories have been observed in all three domains of life (Li et al., 2020), yet the functional advantage(s) of this relationship are unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Slow growing bacterial cells often display a single replication focus, suggesting that sister replisomes are often localized within a single complex.
source: First in B. subtilis (Lemon and Grossman, 1998), and then other bacteria (Brendler et al., 2000; Jensen et al., 2001), it was shown that slow growing cells often displayed a single replication focus, suggesting that sister replisomes are often localized within a single complex.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies in B. subtilis and other bacteria (Lemon and Grossman, 1998; Brendler et al., 2000; Jensen et al., 2001).

claim: Sister replisomes in slow growing bacteria are initially colocalized but then separate into two distinct foci part way through the replication period.
source: Analysis of replisome lifecycles by synchronization or time-lapse microscopy suggests that sister replisomes are initially colocalized but then separate into two distinct foci part way through the replication period (Bates and Kleckner, 2005; Hiraga et al., 2000; Japaridze et al., 2020; Onogi et al., 2002; Reyes-Lamothe et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies using synchronization or time-lapse microscopy (Bates and Kleckner, 2005; Hiraga et al., 2000; Japaridze et al., 2020; Onogi et al., 2002; Reyes-Lamothe et al., 2008).

claim: Under slow growth conditions, replisomes undergo a programmed splitting event one-quarter to one-half of the way through the replication period.
source: This suggests that, at least under slow growth conditions, replisomes undergo a programmed splitting event one-quarter to one-half of the way through the replication period (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the cited studies and is illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Sister replisome splitting is contemporaneous with segregation of the origin region of the chromosome.
source: The mechanism and regulation of sister replisome splitting are unknown, but splitting is contemporaneous with segregation of the origin region of the chromosome (Bates and Kleckner, 2005), which is held together by topological linkages known as precatenanes (Joshi et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bates and Kleckner, 2005.

claim: The origin region of the chromosome is held together by topological linkages known as precatenanes.
source: The mechanism and regulation of sister replisome splitting are unknown, but splitting is contemporaneous with segregation of the origin region of the chromosome (Bates and Kleckner, 2005), which is held together by topological linkages known as precatenanes (Joshi et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Joshi et al., 2013 and Wang et al., 2005.

claim: Bulk measurements of replication foci in rapidly growing E. coli cells indicate that the total number of replication foci is about half the number of replication forks estimated from flow cytometry.
source: Bulk measurements of replication foci in rapidly growing Escherichia coli cells indicate that the total number of replication foci is about half the number of replication forks estimated from flow cytometry (Fossum et al., 2007; Molina and Skarstad, 2004; Sánchez-Romero et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies measuring replication foci (Fossum et al., 2007; Molina and Skarstad, 2004; Sánchez-Romero et al., 2011).

claim: In E. coli, each replisome can function as an independent unit.
source: In E. coli, it is clear that each replisome can function as an independent unit, as blocking one replication fork with either an ectopic terminus (Breier et al., 2005) or array of transcription factor binding sites (Possoz et al., 2006), does not prevent the unblocked replisome from finishing.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies showing that blocking one fork does not prevent the other from finishing (Breier et al., 2005; Possoz et al., 2006).

claim: In S. pombe, a double strand break on one side of an origin does not prevent replication by the opposite-side replisome.
source: Similarly, in S. pombe, a double strand break on one side of an origin does not prevent replication by the opposite-side replisome (Doksani et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Doksani et al., 2009.

claim: Fork stalling at a site of strong transcription oriented toward the oncoming fork in S. cerevisiae causes a significant impairment in progression of the sister replisome.
source: For example, fork stalling at a site of strong transcription oriented toward the oncoming fork in S. cerevisiae was shown to cause a significant impairment in progression of the sister replisome (Brambati et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Brambati et al., 2018.

claim: In both yeast and human cells, sister replisomes exhibit highly coordinate velocities while replisomes initiated from different origins do not.
source: Also, in both yeast (Natsume and Tanaka, 2010) and human (Conti et al., 2007) cells, sister replisomes exhibit highly coordinate velocities while replisomes initiated from different origins do not.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies in yeast (Natsume and Tanaka, 2010) and human cells (Conti et al., 2007).

claim: Immobilizing both ends of the templated DNA leads to a disconnect between sister replisome velocities.
source: Coordinate sister replisome progression is apparently also dependent on colocalization of the forks, as immobilizing both ends of the templated DNA (forcing sister replisomes to separate) leads to a disconnect between sister replisome velocities (Yardimci et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yardimci et al., 2010.

claim: Under slow growth conditions, >99% of E. coli cells contained either 0, 1, or 2 SSB-YPet foci per cell.
source: Quantification of resolvable SSB-YPet foci in >3000 slowly growing cells (τ = 125 min) indicated that >99% of cells contained either 0, 1, or 2 foci per cell (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is based on quantification of SSB-YPet foci in >3000 cells, as shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Under slow growth conditions, the optimal duration of replisome pairing was found to be 20 min.
source: Splitting model distributions more closely matched SSB-YPet, with optimal duration of replisome pairing found to be 20 min (D = 0.04; Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is based on modeling analysis comparing theoretical and observed focus distributions, as shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Under fast growth conditions, the optimal sister replisome pairing time is between 13 and 21 min.
source: Thus, including both splitting and splitting with cousins models, we estimate that that sister replisomes are paired between 13 and 21 min under fast growth conditions and about 20 min under slow growth conditions.
evidence: The claim is based on modeling analysis comparing theoretical and observed focus distributions under fast growth conditions.

claim: Sister replisome pairing intervals correspond to 32–51% of the replication period.
source: These intervals correspond to 32–51% of the replication period.
evidence: The claim is based on calculation from the estimated pairing times and the length of the replication period.

claim: A sister replisome splitting time of 20 min corresponds to a genetic position about 1 Mb from the origin.
source: A sister replisome splitting time of 20 min corresponds to a genetic position about 1 Mb from the origin.
evidence: The claim is based on calculation from the splitting time and fork velocity.

claim: Under slow growth conditions, blocking one replisome at oriC-proximal positions (+0.13 and +0.34 Mb) resulted in a 39 ± 5% reduction in fork progression of the unblocked replisome relative to cells with an oriC-distal roadblock (+1.10 Mb).
source: Slope analysis suggests that fork progression was reduced by 39 ± 5% in cells with an oriC-proximal roadblock relative to cells with an oriC-distal roadblock (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is based on slope analysis of sequencing profiles from roadblocked cells under slow growth conditions, as shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Under fast growth conditions, oriC-proximal blocked cells had on average a 43 ± 7% reduction in fork progression of the unblocked replisome relative to distal blocked cells.
source: We observed a similar difference between oriC-proximal and oriC-distal roadblocked cells, under fast growth conditions, with proximal blocked cells having on average a 43 ± 7% reduction in fork progression of the unblocked replisome relative to distal blocked cells (Figure 3D, E).
evidence: The claim is based on slope analysis of sequencing profiles from roadblocked cells under fast growth conditions, as shown in Figure 3D and 3E.

claim: All roadblocks within ~0.6 Mb from oriC resulted in reduced progression of the unblocked replisome, while all roadblocks downstream of ~0.6 Mb had negligible effect on progression.
source: Additional roadblock positions were tested at +0.32, +0.58, and +0.63 Mb from oriC, the results showing that all roadblocks within ~0.6 Mb from oriC resulted in reduced progression of the unblocked replisome, while all roadblocks downstream of ~0.6 Mb had negligible effect on progression.
evidence: The claim is based on sequencing data from multiple roadblock positions tested under fast growth conditions.

claim: Reduced fork progression in oriC-proximal blocked cells was observed regardless of whether the blocking array was placed on the left or right chromosome arm.
source: Importantly, reduced fork progression in oriC-proximal blocked cells was observed regardless of whether the blocking array was placed on the left or right chromosome arm (−0.35 Mb strain), strongly suggesting that the replication defect was not due to reduced copy number of a specific gene or region.
evidence: The claim is based on sequencing data from roadblocks placed on different chromosome arms.

claim: Unblocked cells achieved 90% runout by 53 ± 4 min.
source: Quantifying flow cytometry histograms via KS analysis (Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2), we find that unblocked cells achieved 90% runout by 53 ± 4 min (Figure 4B, top panel).
evidence: The claim is based on flow cytometry data analyzed by KS analysis, as shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The two oriC-proximal blocked strains did not achieve 90% runout until 70 ± 3 min.
source: Conversely, the two oriC-proximal blocked strains did not achieve 90% runout until 70 ± 3 min (Figure 4B, middle panel), while both oriC-distal blocked strains behaved similarly to unblocked cells, achieving 90% runout by 56 ± 5 min (bottom panel).
evidence: The claim is based on flow cytometry data analyzed by KS analysis, as shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Both oriC-distal blocked strains achieved 90% runout by 56 ± 5 min.
source: Conversely, the two oriC-proximal blocked strains did not achieve 90% runout until 70 ± 3 min (Figure 4B, middle panel), while both oriC-distal blocked strains behaved similarly to unblocked cells, achieving 90% runout by 56 ± 5 min (bottom panel).
evidence: The claim is based on flow cytometry data analyzed by KS analysis, as shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Relative to cells not receiving a roadblock, there was a 32 ± 3% reduction in replication speed when one arm was blocked near the origin.
source: Relative to cells not receiving a roadblock, this equates to a 32 ± 3% reduction in replication speed when one arm was blocked near the origin, versus a negligible reduction (3 ± 3%) in replication speed when one arm was blocked ≥0.6 Mb from the origin (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is based on flow cytometry data analyzed by KS analysis, as shown in Figure 4C.

claim: There was a negligible reduction (3 ± 3%) in replication speed when one arm was blocked ≥0.6 Mb from the origin.
source: Relative to cells not receiving a roadblock, this equates to a 32 ± 3% reduction in replication speed when one arm was blocked near the origin, versus a negligible reduction (3 ± 3%) in replication speed when one arm was blocked ≥0.6 Mb from the origin (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is based on flow cytometry data analyzed by KS analysis, as shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Fork stalling is a frequent event in wild-type cells, with replisome dissociation estimates as high as 4–5 times per replication cycle.
source: Fork stalling is a frequent event in wild-type cells, with replisome dissociation estimates as high as 4–5 times per replication cycle (Mangiameli et al., 2017a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mangiameli et al., 2017a.

claim: An estimated 5–20% of stalled forks experience breakage by shearing or collision from a second fork, forming a collapsed fork.
source: Although the majority of stalled forks are restarted quickly via PriA-mediated reloading of the replicative helicase, an estimated 5–20% experience breakage by shearing or collision from a second fork, forming a so-called broken or collapsed fork, which requires recombination-mediated strand invasion steps to reestablish a fork structure (Courcelle et al., 2015; Michel et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Courcelle et al., 2015 and Michel et al., 2018.

claim: Cells with no roadblock experienced 4 ± 1% fork stalling.
source: Cells with no roadblock experienced 4 ± 1% fork stalling.
evidence: The claim is based on sequencing data from recB− cells after rifampicin runout.

claim: oriC-proximal roadblocking resulted in 21 ± 3% and 26 ± 2% fork stalling.
source: Quantifying percent replication fork stalling as the fraction of forks on the unblocked chromosome arm in recB− cells that remained after rifampicin runout (Materials and methods), we found that oriC-proximal roadblocking resulted in 21 ± 3% and 26 ± 2% fork stalling, while oriC-distal roadblocking resulted in only 5 ± 1% fork stalling (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is based on sequencing data from recB− cells after rifampicin runout, as shown in Figure 5B.

claim: oriC-distal roadblocking resulted in only 5 ± 1% fork stalling.
source: Quantifying percent replication fork stalling as the fraction of forks on the unblocked chromosome arm in recB− cells that remained after rifampicin runout (Materials and methods), we found that oriC-proximal roadblocking resulted in 21 ± 3% and 26 ± 2% fork stalling, while oriC-distal roadblocking resulted in only 5 ± 1% fork stalling (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is based on sequencing data from recB− cells after rifampicin runout, as shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Holliday junctions are four-way DNA junctions formed at stalled forks by either regression of the fork and subsequent annealing of the newly replicated strands, or by homologous recombination during fork remodeling.
source: HJs are four-way DNA junctions formed at stalled forks by either regression of the fork and subsequent annealing of the newly replicated strands (Atkinson and McGlynn, 2009), or by homologous recombination during fork remodeling (Michel et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Atkinson and McGlynn, 2009 and Michel et al., 2018.

claim: Holliday junctions are hallmarks of stalled forks.
source: Thus, HJs are hallmarks of stalled forks, which are effectively detected by RDG (Xia et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Xia et al., 2016.

claim: Orphaned replisomes experienced 50 ± 9% more stalling than wild-type replisomes in oriC-distal blocked cells (+1.10 Mb).
source: This analysis indicates that orphaned replisomes experienced 50 ± 9% more stalling that wild-type replisomes in oriC-distal blocked cells (+1.10 Mb) and 116 ± 6% more stalling than wild-type replisomes in oriC-proximal blocked cells (+0.13 and +0.34 Mb).
evidence: The claim is based on RDG ChIP-seq data from roadblocked cells.

claim: Orphaned replisomes experienced 116 ± 6% more stalling than wild-type replisomes in oriC-proximal blocked cells (+0.13 and +0.34 Mb).
source: This analysis indicates that orphaned replisomes experienced 50 ± 9% more stalling that wild-type replisomes in oriC-distal blocked cells (+1.10 Mb) and 116 ± 6% more stalling than wild-type replisomes in oriC-proximal blocked cells (+0.13 and +0.34 Mb).
evidence: The claim is based on RDG ChIP-seq data from roadblocked cells.

claim: Replisomes orphaned soon after replication initiation stalled significantly more than replisomes orphaned late in the replication period.
source: Thus, replisomes orphaned soon after replication initiation stalled significantly more than replisomes orphaned late in the replication period.
evidence: The claim is based on RDG ChIP-seq data from roadblocked cells at different positions.

claim: About 30 hotspots of RDG binding were identified on the unblocked chromosome arm in oriC-proximal blocked cells, with ~80% of peaks shared among the two strains.
source: Identification of the major peaks of RDG binding revealed about 30 hotspots on the unblocked chromosome arm in oriC-proximal blocked cells, with ~80% of peaks shared among the two strains (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of RDG ChIP-seq data, as shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: RDG peaks were dispersed along the unblocked arm, implying that fork collapse was not restricted to regions that are normally replicated by colocalized sister replisomes.
source: Interestingly, RDG peaks were dispersed along the unblocked arm, implying that fork collapse was not restricted to regions that are normally replicated by colocalized sister replisomes.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the distribution of RDG peaks observed in ChIP-seq data.

claim: E. coli sister replisomes exhibit inter-dependent behavior during the early stages of DNA replication.
source: Our data indicate that E. coli sister replisomes exhibit inter-dependent behavior during the early stages of DNA replication.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding, supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Blocking one replisome within ~0.6 Mb of oriC negatively influenced the sister replisome, resulting in poorer overall fork progression measured by deep sequencing and reduced fork velocity by timed rifampicin runout.
source: Blocking one replisome within ~0.6 Mb of oriC negatively influenced the sister replisome, resulting in poorer overall fork progression measured by deep sequencing and reduced fork velocity by timed rifampicin runout.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding, supported by the sequencing and flow cytometry data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Prematurely split replisomes were six times less likely to complete replication without the restart protein RecB.
source: Such prematurely split replisomes were six times less likely to complete replication without the restart protein RecB and produced twice as many HJs as control cells, indicating increased fork stalling.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding, supported by the sequencing data from recB− cells and RDG ChIP-seq data.

claim: Prematurely split replisomes produced twice as many HJs as control cells, indicating increased fork stalling.
source: Such prematurely split replisomes were six times less likely to complete replication without the restart protein RecB and produced twice as many HJs as control cells, indicating increased fork stalling.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding, supported by the RDG ChIP-seq data.

claim: Fork barriers placed farther than 0.6 Mb from the origin had minimal effect on progression of the unblocked replisome.
source: Fork barriers placed farther than 0.6 Mb from the origin had minimal effect on progression of the unblocked replisome, suggesting that sister replisomes transition to a fully independent state part way through replication.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding, supported by the sequencing and flow cytometry data.

claim: Sister replisomes transition to a fully independent state part way through replication.
source: Fork barriers placed farther than 0.6 Mb from the origin had minimal effect on progression of the unblocked replisome, suggesting that sister replisomes transition to a fully independent state part way through replication.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that distal roadblocks have minimal effect on the unblocked replisome.

claim: The functional transition point roughly coincides with a physical transition of the replication machinery from colocalized (factory) replisomes to fully separate complexes.
source: Fluorescence imaging showed that this functional transition point roughly coincides with a physical transition of the replication machinery from colocalized (factory) replisomes to fully separate complexes.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding, supported by the fluorescence imaging data and the roadblocking experiments.

claim: Replication fork progression through approximately the first third of the chromosome is facilitated by a physical association of leftward and rightward sister replisomes.
source: We conclude that replication fork progression through approximately the first third of the chromosome is facilitated by a physical association of leftward and rightward sister replisomes.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the combined data from fluorescence imaging, sequencing, and flow cytometry experiments.

claim: In both yeast and human cells, sister replisomes, but not replisomes initiated from different origins, exhibit similar velocities.
source: In both yeast (Natsume and Tanaka, 2010) and human cells (Conti et al., 2007), sister replisomes, but not replisomes initiated from different origins, exhibit similar velocities and blocking one fork with strong head-on transcription inhibits progression of its sister fork (Brambati et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies in yeast (Natsume and Tanaka, 2010) and human cells (Conti et al., 2007).

claim: Blocking one fork with strong head-on transcription inhibits progression of its sister fork.
source: In both yeast (Natsume and Tanaka, 2010) and human cells (Conti et al., 2007), sister replisomes, but not replisomes initiated from different origins, exhibit similar velocities and blocking one fork with strong head-on transcription inhibits progression of its sister fork (Brambati et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Brambati et al., 2018.

claim: The data are not at odds with a previous E. coli study concluding that sister replisomes are independent.
source: Notably, our data are not at odds with a those of a previous E. coli study concluding that sister replisomes are independent (Breier et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a statement reconciling the current findings with a previous study.

claim: The previous E. coli study used an ectopic termination site placed ~1 Mb from oriC, in a region that would be expected to have little effect on the unblocked replisome.
source: That study used an ectopic termination site to block one replisome; however, the block was placed ~1 Mb from oriC, thus in a region that we would expect to have little effect on the unblocked replisome.
evidence: This is an explanation for why the previous study did not observe interdependence, based on the current findings.

claim: Colocalizing replisomes may facilitate replication by increasing the local concentration of resources at the fork.
source: Colocalizing replisomes may facilitate replication simply by increasing the local concentration of resources at the fork.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the functional advantage of replication factories.

claim: Most replication components have been shown to localize or interact with the replisome.
source: Most of these components have been shown to localize or interact with the replisome (Bentchikou et al., 2015; López de Saro and O'Donnell, 2001; Sánchez-Romero et al., 2011; Stracy et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies showing localization or interaction of replication components with the replisome (Bentchikou et al., 2015; López de Saro and O'Donnell, 2001; Sánchez-Romero et al., 2011; Stracy et al., 2019).

claim: Conservation of the spatial distribution of replication resources to a defined volume around the replisomes would promote efficient fork progression.
source: It is reasonable to assume that conservation of the spatial distribution of replication resources to a defined volume around the replisomes would promote efficient fork progression, especially in a large cell or nucleus.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the functional advantage of replication factories.

claim: Factory replication may be important for coordinating the timing of left and right replication forks.
source: Alternatively, factory replication may be important for coordinating the timing of left and right replication forks.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the functional advantage of replication factories.

claim: For organisms with circular chromosomes and a single replication origin, precise convergence of forks at the terminus is critical for chromosome segregation and resolution of chromosome dimers.
source: For organisms with circular chromosomes and a single replication origin, precise convergence of forks at the terminus is critical for chromosome segregation and resolution of chromosome dimers (Dimude et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dimude et al., 2016.

claim: Most forks converge within a very narrow termination zone near the dif site, implying that movement of sister replisomes is tightly coordinated.
source: Even though many bacteria possess emergency replication fork traps to limit extensive overtravel, most forks converge within a very narrow termination zone near the dif site (Hendrickson and Lawrence, 2007), implying that movement of sister replisomes is tightly coordinated.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hendrickson and Lawrence, 2007, and the inference is based on the observation of precise fork convergence.

claim: Coordinating sister replisome travel may provide a mechanism for equal transfer of epigenetic marks such as histones.
source: While it is unclear if coordinating termination of sister replisomes would confer any advantage in organisms with linear chromosomes since fork convergence occurs between forks initiated at different origins, coordinating sister replisome travel may provide a mechanism for equal transfer of epigenetic marks such as histones (Yuan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the functional advantage of coordinating sister replisome travel, supported by a citation to Yuan et al., 2019.

claim: Factories may be important for fork progression through impediments including bound protein and transcription complexes.
source: Lastly, factories may be important for fork progression through impediments including bound protein and transcription complexes.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the functional advantage of replication factories.

claim: If sister replisomes are anchored to a cell structure or to each other via a stable link, the resulting complex might stabilize replisomes against mechanical stress imposed on the replicative helicase as it travels through dense chromatin.
source: If sister replisomes are anchored to a cell structure such as a nuclear or cell membrane, or to each other via a stable link, the resulting complex might stabilize replisomes against mechanical stress imposed on the replicative helicase as it travels through dense chromatin.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the functional advantage of replication factories.

claim: Up to 70% of all transcription in E. coli, including the highly active ribosomal genes, occurs within the ori-proximal ~1/3 of the chromosome.
source: Supporting this idea, up to 70% of all transcription in E. coli, including the highly active ribosomal genes, occurs within the ori-proximal ~1/3 of the chromosome (Grainger et al., 2006), matching closely the region in which sister replisomes are colocalized (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Grainger et al., 2006.

claim: The region where up to 70% of all transcription occurs matches closely the region in which sister replisomes are colocalized.
source: Supporting this idea, up to 70% of all transcription in E. coli, including the highly active ribosomal genes, occurs within the ori-proximal ~1/3 of the chromosome (Grainger et al., 2006), matching closely the region in which sister replisomes are colocalized (Figure 2).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the transcription data from Grainger et al., 2006 with the replisome colocalization data from Figure 2.

claim: Early models of replication proposed that bidirectional replisomes exist in an obligate binary configuration in which the two helicases are oriented head-to-head.
source: Early models of replication proposed that bidirectional replisomes exist in an obligate binary configuration in which the two helicases are oriented head-to-head (Dingman, 1974).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dingman, 1974.

claim: In the obligate binary configuration, one replisome copies the top strand and one replisome copies the bottom strand.
source: In this configuration, one replisome copies the top strand and one replisome copies the bottom strand, and thus the two replisomes are unable to separate without either (1) pulling Watson away from Crick, or (2) completely dissociating and reassociating both replisomes (Bates, 2008) including DnaB helicase, which is thought to remain stably associated throughout replication (Monachino et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a description of the obligate binary configuration model, supported by citations to Bates, 2008 and Monachino et al., 2020.

claim: DnaB helicase is thought to remain stably associated throughout replication.
source: In this configuration, one replisome copies the top strand and one replisome copies the bottom strand, and thus the two replisomes are unable to separate without either (1) pulling Watson away from Crick, or (2) completely dissociating and reassociating both replisomes (Bates, 2008) including DnaB helicase, which is thought to remain stably associated throughout replication (Monachino et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Monachino et al., 2020.

claim: Given that sister replisome splitting occurs naturally in bacteria and under forced conditions in eukaryotes, an obligate factory complex seems unlikely.
source: Given that sister replisome splitting occurs naturally in bacteria (Bates and Kleckner, 2005; Berkmen and Grossman, 2006; Hiraga et al., 2000; Japaridze et al., 2020; Mangiameli et al., 2017b; Onogi et al., 2002; Reyes-Lamothe et al., 2008) and under forced conditions in eukaryotes (Brambati et al., 2018; Yardimci et al., 2010), such an obligate factory complex seems unlikely.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of sister replisome splitting in bacteria and eukaryotes, supported by multiple citations.

claim: The eukaryotic Ctf4 protein can dimerize CMG helicase between two replisomes forming a stable factory.
source: One such protein is the eukaryotic Ctf4 protein, which can dimerize CMG helicase between two replisomes forming a stable factory (Yuan et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yuan et al., 2019.

claim: Ctf4 may direct the lagging strands from both replisomes to a single shared Pol α primase, which would coordinate bidirectional synthesis.
source: Ctf4 may also direct the lagging strands from both replisomes to a single shared Pol α primase, which would coordinate bidirectional synthesis (Li et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2020.

claim: No analogous tethering protein has been identified in bacteria.
source: Although no analogous tethering protein has been identified in bacteria, there are fork-associated proteins capable of crosslinking, which might link sister replisomes if bound in sufficient quantities.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Candidate proteins for linking sister replisomes include SeqA in E. coli, YabA in B. subtilis, and GapA in C. crescentus.
source: Candidate proteins include one of the highly abundant fork-associated proteins found in bacteria; SeqA in E. coli, YabA in B. subtilis, and GapA in C. crescentus.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the properties of these proteins.

claim: SeqA, YabA, and GapA can form polymers and some mutants exhibit reduced fork progression and aberrant replisome dynamics.
source: These proteins can form polymers and some mutants exhibit reduced fork progression and aberrant replisome dynamics (Arias-Cartin et al., 2017; Fossum et al., 2007; Joshi et al., 2013; Soufo et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies showing that these proteins can form polymers and that mutants exhibit replication defects (Arias-Cartin et al., 2017; Fossum et al., 2007; Joshi et al., 2013; Soufo et al., 2008).

claim: Sister replisomes are connected indirectly via entanglements of newly replicated DNA exiting the forks.
source: In contrast to protein linker models, we propose that sister replisomes are instead connected indirectly via entanglements of newly replicated DNA exiting the forks.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal for how sister replisomes are linked.

claim: Topological stress at the fork totals 100 duplex twists per second at an elongation rate of 1000 bp per second.
source: Topological stress at the fork, totaling 100 duplex twists per second at an elongation rate of 1000 bp per second, are reduced by topoisomerases and diluted by diffusion (as supercoils) into the surrounding DNA.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the elongation rate and the helical pitch of DNA.

claim: Excess topological stress routinely builds to the point that DNA around the fork becomes entwined and highly condensed.
